It's more of the same circular reasoning we find everywhere in psychiatry and neuroscientific commentary when it comes to religion. First, they take the irrationality and destructiveness of religion as self-evident, and then they argue how religion arose from folk psychology. Then to make their arguments for how these beliefs form, they use folk psychological theories.

Note his use of the phrase imagination throughout this lecture. This isn't yet a neuroscientific concept. So many of these popular atheistic writers are fine referring to 'neuroscience', when what they're really doing is cherry-picking from a confused mixture of their favorite concepts from psychology, neuroscience, and philosophy. Neuroscience describes phenomena in terms of the behavior of neurons and cognitive abstractions. It has no place for imagination, at least without making the sorts of leaps into folk psychology that these speakers are prone to. So at one and the same time, they tend to be dismissive of folk psychological theories, but then they use folk psychological explanations to make their neuroscientific cases.

Thomson wants to argue that religious belief is just a byproduct, an accident of social imagination and hyperactive agency seeking. This reasoning is the victim of a mistaken historicity where mankind - just 3 or 4 millennia ago - were a bunch of drooling idiots rubbing their dicks in circles in the dirt to make magic weather happen. It's fucking ridiculous. The evidence for religious belief is not evidence that ancient peoples were far less rational than we are today. They had complex economies and social structures, were working with rudimentary algebras and geometries, had linguistic/numeral systems and systems for writing, as well as complex legal systems. They'd calculated patterns of motion of objects in space with an amazing degree of precision, given the tools they had.

Yet, we're supposed to believe these people were haphazardly, and unconsciously, extending normal cognitive adaptations to generating pure superstition.

One other problem is the conflation of cognitive processes with mental states (such as belief states). He does this throughout the talk. Cognitive processes are supposed to lead to cognitive states, but what these terms really refer to are mental states. Why should we think that physicalist cognitive processes could over-extend and produce imaginative mental states that generate grossly irrational behaviors? If that's the case with religion, it would stand out uniquely among all of our drives/instincts. I've already mentioned that the idea of imagination being a purely cognitive function is very controversial. We don't have a good reason to think that imagination is explainable by the regular appeal to cognition in terms of computation, which is the general (if unspoken) spirit behind these talks about cognition.

Take the example Thomson uses about energy balance. It seems reasonable that there are cognitive processes for interpreting energy balance in the body. These would cause us to seek energy-dense foods during times of energy instability. Some functional learning process would cause individuals and cultures to recognize properties about the highest-energy foodstuff.

Does that directedness toward the highest energy-density cause men to both (a) imagine an infinite energy food and (b) come to believe it exists in reality?

Is there historical demonstration of widespread cultural belief in the infinite energy food? Of course there isn't. But, why then, are we supposed to think that social imagination and agency-seeking would cause mankind to believe in the infinite, transcendent person just because we could imagine it? It has as much veracity (or plausibility) as the infinite energy food does. Yet no ancient culture appeared to reflect belief in an infinite energy food.

The fact is, you could overextend most cognitive processes and say that the imaginative function might supernaturally maximize the target of that process. I also like to sleep. People seek out opportunities to sleep, and sometimes when they're very exhausted they imagine sleeping. Does that cause us to think that the objects of our imagination are real? We desire sex most of the time as well...does this cause us to form the belief that there is an immaterial sexual reality out there? Of course not.

Thomson uses the example of McDonalds as evidence for this "supernormal" satisfaction of desires. It's terrible reasoning. So, since man discovered ways to concentrate chemical energy in garbage food, this is somehow evidence that we always find ways to satisfy the imaginative over-extension of our cognitive processes? If I can't maximize my urge to sleep empirically, then I do it superstitiously. If I can't maximize the satisfaction of my sex drive, then my imagining sex causes me to assume that perfect sex exists immaterially outside of me? It runs contrary to common sense and empirical reality. Humans have mostly recognized the tension between their imaginations and reality, i.e. the stifling of our wants by limitations of our bodies and the world. Do we really believe that ancient peoples didn't recognize that we don't just get what we want?

I think this is so obvious that it makes Thomson's position non-serious. We can study the body and human culture and find that in both, we have evolved mechanisms for limiting drive satisfaction, and for tempering the imagination - that is, we have elaborate machinery for limiting the cognitive processes themselves that inspire imagination. Human culture serves this function itself - we establish complex narratives for how to approach life, and we treat individuals whose wishful thinking is unreasonable as having mental pathologies. Evolution itself operates to constantly couple our beliefs to reality as much as possible - where they are in great conflict, it tends to kill people.

Now you've got to answer the question why, if these religious structures were so irrational, did they evolve ubiquitously and independently in every human society in recorded history? Why were they preserved if irrationality is supposedly leading to maladaptive and destructive things? It begs the entire question: if what Thomson is saying is true, why should we even think that rationality is the optimization of cognitive processing. All that empirical reality is doing to Thomson's argument is demonstrating that irrationality obviously serves some very high order function that is preservative to human societies.

In my argument, I had as a premise that ancient cultures did not have any popular concepts of an infinite energy food. I don't like working against my own arguments, but the idea hit me literally as I was waking up this morning:

Soma

Soma was a Hindu concept, an elixir that granted immortality. Like Ambrosia, it has been identified in certain places as either a drink or a dish. Some contemporary thinkers have a theory that all of these ancient immortality-granting foods were really entheogens.

Ambrosia occurred to me shortly thereafter. And then the Philosopher's Stone.

And also, the Eucharist. I really don't know how I missed that one as I was typing those words yesterday, other than to say that we were looking at the origins of beliefs. I want to say that most of these concepts postdate the belief in Gods and deities. So they present a challenge to the concept that God arose as a belief from something like amplification of "imaginative perfection", or like a frame shift from the perfect material to the perfect immaterial. Once we have the belief in divinity, it's not a struggle to see how we get to divine stuff.

Plato's Forms also occur to me, so according to him there was basically a perfection of all sensible things.

Obviously the Philosopher's Stone and the Eucharist are relatively late in the game; the former much, much later. Still, it is interesting to see how notions of divinity in objects changed over time. We tend to move away from food and drink toward things that are more symbolic of technology. Anyway, Plato stands out as a genius weirdo because somehow during the 4th century B.C. he's envisioning an abstract, perfect geometric form for everything, which is so far ahead of his time it's astonishing. I think Tegmark is pretty much arguing this today.

But maybe my argument still hits the main vein. I don't know. It feels very weakened. The Ontological Argument also comes to mind. Anselm wanted to do the exact opposite of what Thomson is doing in this lecture. Anselm wanted to say that whatever our cognitive processes are that allow us to conceive of perfection itself are proof of God's existence. Thomson seems like he is, maybe inadvertently, turning this around on Anselm: no, there is a cognitive psychological basis for our tendency to perfect things in the mind, and we started by defeating death imaginatively through postmortem ancestor worship.

There is some really interesting tie between the idea of consumption and immortality in the Eucharist, some very ancient idea that was carried over into Christianity, but the connection isn't clear to me.

Anyway, I don't want to ramble. If anybody has any thought on this, whether it supports or takes down my original premise, then chime in. I know this is kind of all over the place.
